TM Data Quality Analyzer

User Manual — Version 2.9.3

TM Data Quality Analyzer examines IRIG 106 Chapter 10 PCM telemetry recordings and plots two data-quality metrics over time, per stream:

  • Frame Sync Lock — the percentage of each time window the decommutator held frame lock, plus a running count of missed frames.
  • Receiver AGC/SNR — receiver signal metrics embedded in the PCM frame, optionally converted to dB through a calibration profile.

1. Before you process: the two setup dialogs

Every stream you process is configured through the gear button on its row in Configure Streams. Which dialog opens depends on the row's Mode. Getting these fields right is the difference between a meaningful plot and a confident-looking wrong one, so they are worth understanding before the walkthroughs that use them.

Configure Frame Sync Lock

FieldWhat it isWhat a wrong value does
Frame Sync The synchronisation pattern in hex, up to 64 bits. No frames are found at all. The log says the pattern was not located and the stream plots as a flat zero.
Frame Sync Mask Which bits of the pattern must match. FFFFFFFF means all of them. Too permissive a mask matches noise, so lock % reads high on a stream that is not really locked.
Bits Per Frame The minor frame length in bits. The scanner looks for the next sync in the wrong place. You typically see syncs found but few or no frames extracted.
Data Rate (Mbps) The stream's bit rate. Very little — see the note below.
Average Period The window each lock % figure is computed over: 1 s, 100 ms or 10 ms. Nothing is wrong, but a longer window smooths over brief dropouts and a shorter one produces far more points.
Derandomize Undo RNRZ-L randomisation before searching for the pattern. On a randomised stream, leaving this off means the pattern is never found. Turning it on for a stream that is not randomised has the same effect.
Invert Data Invert every bit before decoding. As above: an inverted stream left un-inverted finds no syncs.
Lock % does not depend on an exact data rate. It is measured as a proportion of the frame-sized bit slots actually traversed, not as time × bitrate. A slightly wrong Data Rate will not skew the percentage. The field is there because the value is genuinely useful elsewhere, not because the metric is fragile.
Load and Save round-trip only three fields. The folder and disk buttons write Frame Sync, Frame Sync Mask and Bits Per Frame, and nothing else. Derandomize, Data Rate and Average Period are deliberately treated as per-session choices and are not saved. This is intended, not an oversight: a pattern file describes a frame format, which is a property of the telemetry, while the others describe how you happen to be looking at it today. If you reload a file and those toggles are back at their defaults, nothing was lost.

Configure Receiver SNR

The top half is identical to the frame sync dialog and behaves the same way — an SNR stream still has to be frame-synchronised before anything can be read out of it. The lower half describes the receiver data:

FieldWhat it isWhat a wrong value does
Num Rcvrs and Num Channels How many receivers the frame carries, and how many channels each has (typically three: left, right, combined). Their product is the total channel count. Reading the wrong words out of the frame, so curves appear that are really other channels' data.
Polarity Whether the raw count rises or falls with signal strength. An upside-down plot: signal increases read as decreases.
Slope The receiver's output voltage range — 0–5 V, 0–10 V, ±5 V or ±10 V. Values scaled by a constant factor. The shape is right, the numbers are not.
Scale (dB/V) How many decibels one volt represents. As above — a linear error through every value.

The Apply Cal button, and the status text beside it, belong to non-linear step calibration. Until you attach a profile it reads (none — using linear calibration), meaning values are converted with the slope and scale above and nothing else. The calibration walkthrough below covers what that costs and how to improve it.

Apply to all at the bottom of either dialog copies these settings to every other selected stream of the same mode. On a file with sixteen identical receiver streams this turns sixteen configuration passes into one.

2. Walkthrough: frame sync lock

The goal: take a Chapter 10 recording, measure how well each PCM stream held frame synchronisation, and find the moments where it did not.

Step 1 — Open the recording

Use ≡ → Open… (or Ctrl+O), or drag a .ch10 file onto the window.

The application reads the file's TMATS metadata — not the data itself, which is why this is quick even on a multi-gigabyte recording — and opens the Configure Streams dialog listing every PCM channel it found.

Step 2 — Choose which streams to process, and how

For each stream you want to measure, switch Process on and leave Mode at Frame Sync Lock. Then open its gear dialog and fill in the frame sync fields described in Before you process.

Watch the Ready column as you go. It is the dialog telling you whether it has enough information to run:

  • ✓ — configured and ready to process.
  • ✗ — selected for processing but not yet configured. Open the gear dialog.
  • ✗ — not selected. Nothing is required of it.

Also set the Time Channel at the top. Every stream is timestamped from it, so all the curves share one time axis.

Step 3 — Process

Press Process. The file is read once, with every selected stream decoded in parallel, so processing four streams costs little more than processing one.

The log is worth reading rather than ignoring. Each stream reports the bytes it processed, the syncs it found and the frames it extracted — the quickest way to notice that a stream was misconfigured is a large sync count with almost no frames.

Step 4 — Read the plot

The left axis is the percentage of each averaging window in which the stream held lock. There is no right-hand axis here because this recording carries no receiver data — an axis appears only when something is plotted against it.

Healthy streams sit near 100%. What matters is the cliffs: vertical drops to zero where synchronisation was lost. Their width is how long the outage lasted and their position is when.

Step 5 — Switch to accumulation

Press V, or use the Show Accumulation button on the chart.

Lock % answers "how good was the link at this moment"; accumulation answers "how much data did I actually lose". A stream that dips briefly but often can look worse than one long outage on the percentage plot while costing far fewer frames — the accumulation view settles which is which.

Step 6 — Export

Right-click the chart and choose Export…. You can produce an image, the underlying data as CSV, and the log text in one action; see Import & export for exactly what each contains.

3. Getting started

  1. Open the application menu with the ≡ button at the top left.
  2. Choose Open… (or press Ctrl+O) and select a .ch10 file — or simply drag and drop the file anywhere onto the window. Recently opened files are listed under Recent Files.
  3. The Configure Streams dialog appears, listing every PCM channel found in the recording. Configure the streams you want (see section 2) and press Process.
  4. Processing runs in the background with a progress dialog; results appear on the plot as each stream finishes.

4. Configuring streams

Each PCM channel row in the Configure Streams dialog has:

  • Process — include or exclude the stream from this run.
  • Mode — Frame Sync Lock Stats or Receiver AGC/SNR.
  • Settings (gear) — the per-stream setup dialog:
    • Frame sync: sync pattern, sync mask, and words per frame. These three fields can be saved to / loaded from a TOML file for reuse. Below the separator, Randomized, Data Rate, and Sample Rate are per-session inputs and are not saved.
    • SNR setup (SNR mode): word layout of the receiver channels within the frame, plus inversion/randomization flags.
    • Calibration (SNR mode): extract a calibration profile from a calibration run so raw counts convert to dB. Profiles apply to the current session only — they are never written to disk.

The dialog also selects the time channel used to timestamp all streams, and an optional start/stop time range to restrict processing.

5. Working with the plot

The chart fills the whole plot area — there are no control rows around it. Everything is either right-click on the plot or a small control overlaid on the chart, so the maximum amount of space shows data.

The right-click menu

Right-click anywhere on the chart. Entries stay disabled until a file has been processed.

  • Set Plot Title… — the title shown above the chart and carried into exports.
  • Plot File — after a batch run, picks which file's series are shown, or All files (overlaid). Disabled when only one file is loaded.
  • View Mode (V) — for Frame Sync Lock data, switches the left axis between Lock Percentage and Accumulation (running missed-frame count). Disabled unless the data contains both. The key is shown on the entry itself because it cycles between the two views rather than picking one.
  • Customize View… — rename series, change their colors, and show or hide individual series.
  • Show Legend — same toggle as the on-chart button below.
  • Readout — chooses which series the hover value comes from. Nearest series (automatic) is the default: whichever curve lies closest to the pointer reports its value, which is ambiguous where several series overlap. Pick a series instead to pin the readout to it — from then on the value shown is always that series' value at the cursor's time (marked (pinned)), no matter which curve is nearer. Only series currently on the plot are listed; if a pinned series is hidden or re-processed, the readout reverts to automatic.
  • X Axis → Set Time Window… — type a start and stop time as DDD:HH:MM:SS to zoom to an exact span. Values outside the file's range are clamped to it and a note appears in the log. Reset Span returns to the full time range.
  • Y Axes → Set Left Max… / Set Right Max… — pin the top of the left (lock % or missed frames) or right (SNR dB) axis. Minimums always scale automatically. Reset clears both maximums back to automatic.
  • Reset View R — restores the full time span and automatic axis scaling in one action, exactly as the on-chart Reset view chip does. X Axis → Reset Span and Y Axes → Reset each do half of it.
  • Export… — the same export dialog as the main menu (see Import & export).

On-chart controls

A small chip bar floats at the chart's top-left. It holds only what is useful right now — chips appear and disappear with the state of the plot, so nothing sits there unused.

  • Legend button — shows or hides the legend. Your choice is remembered between sessions, and a hidden legend is also left out of exported images.
  • View Mode chip — one click flips the left axis between Lock % and Accumulation. The chip is labelled with the view it will switch to, and only appears when the data contains both.
  • Reset view chip — appears only once you have zoomed in or pinned an axis maximum; clicking it restores the full time span and automatic scaling.
  • Legend — drag it anywhere inside the chart to keep it clear of the data. It starts in the top-right corner and lists one row per visible series.

Reading values off the plot

  • A dashed crosshair follows the pointer so several series can be compared at the same instant.
  • Hovering near a data point shows its series name, time and value. By default that is the nearest curve; use Readout in the right-click menu to pin it to one series — useful when curves overlap and you always want the same one.

Navigating

  • Zoom — scroll the mouse wheel over the chart to zoom the time axis.
  • Pan — click and drag left/right to move through time. The cursor becomes an open hand over the chart and closes while you drag.
  • Zoom to a range — hold Ctrl and drag (or drag with the middle mouse button) to rubber-band a time span; releasing zooms to exactly that span.
  • Crosshair — a dashed time line follows the cursor so values can be compared across several series at the same instant; the tooltip shows the nearest reading.
  • Back to full view — double-click the chart, click the Reset view chip, or use X Axis → Reset Span.
  • Keyboard — click the chart once to focus it, then single keys drive the view: ← → to step through time, + − to zoom, R to reset. See Keyboard shortcuts for the full list.

6. Understanding the metrics

Frame Sync Lock

Lock % is computed from bits actually observed: within each averaging window it is the share of bits that belonged to frames in lock. Missed frames count loss-of-lock events — the accumulation view shows their running total. A clean recording plots at a flat 100% with a flat accumulation line.

Receiver AGC/SNR

Receiver words embedded in each frame are averaged per window as raw counts, then converted once per window through the calibration profile (if attached). Readings outside the calibrated range clamp to the nearest calibrated step rather than extrapolating.

7. Templates & batch processing

A processing template captures one configured file's complete per-stream setup — modes, frame-sync settings, SNR layout, plus each series' custom name and color — independent of any file path.

Save as Template…

After processing a file, choose Save as Template… from the menu to write the template as a .json file.

Apply Template to Files…

  1. Pick a template file, then select any number of .ch10 files.
  2. Each file is validated up front: its PCM channel-ID set must exactly match the template's. Non-matching files are flagged with the missing/extra channels and skipped.
  3. In the batch dialog, optionally enable per-file export — for every processed file this writes a CSV plus two plot images (…_framesync_lock.png and …_missed_frames.png) to a folder you choose.
  4. All processed files stay loaded; use the Plot File selector to review each one or overlay them all.
Files must contain the same PCM channel IDs as the template. A file with even one extra or missing channel is rejected — this guarantees settings are never silently applied to the wrong physical channel.

8. Import & export

  • Export… — writes the current plot's data to CSV and/or the chart to an image (PNG, SVG, or PDF), and can save the log. Available from the menu and from the plot's right-click menu. A legend you have hidden is left out of exported images.
  • Import CSV… — loads a previously exported CSV straight onto the plot, with no reprocessing. Dropping a .csv onto the window does the same.

9. Interface & settings

  • Menu (≡) — every command lives in the single top-left menu, grouped into Process, Import/Export, Settings, and Help sections.
  • Sidebar — the panel on the left shows the processing log. It is shown by default; toggle it with the sidebar button next to the menu, or Ctrl+B. Its state is remembered between sessions.
  • Plot controls — the plot itself has no surrounding toolbars: right-click the chart for its menu, and use the on-chart legend button. See Working with the plot.
  • Theme — switch between dark and light themes from the Settings section.
  • Status bar — shows the loaded file and processing status.

10. Keyboard shortcuts

Anywhere in the application

ShortcutAction
Ctrl+OOpen a Chapter 10 or CSV file
Ctrl+BShow / hide the sidebar (log)

While the chart has focus

Click the chart once to focus it. These are single keys, so they act only on the chart — they never interfere with typing in a dialog or a configuration field. The right-click menu shows the key next to each command as a reminder.

ShortcutAction
← → Step the visible time window earlier / later, keeping its width
+ − Zoom the time axis in / out about the centre of the view
Home Back to the full time span, keeping any Y axis maximum you set
R Reset the view — full time span and automatic Y axes
V Switch the left axis between Lock % and Accumulation
L Show or hide the legend
